title: Responsive Self Service Procurement in Oracle Fusion
summary: How a requisition in Oracle Fusion's Responsive (Redwood) Self Service Procurement travels from shopping to a paid invoice, and which setup lever controls each step.
objectives: **Trace** a requisition through the six stages: Shop → Cart/Submit → Approve → Buyer → PO → Receipt and Invoice
**Explain** why a requester can't see a catalog (content zones) or can't create requisitions at all (requisitioning BU access, `POR-2010674`)
**Distinguish** where approval *rules* live (Manage Requisition Approvals, AMX) from where approval *task behavior* lives (BPM Worklist)
**Predict** whether an approved line becomes a PO automatically or waits in Process Requisitions
**Name** the setup task behind each stage of the flow

steps.title: The company food court
steps.narration: Picture the food court at a big office. Kitchens cook and stock the dishes. Counters show them: a salad bar, a grill stall run by an outside vendor, and a desk where you fill in a custom order. You walk up as a **diner** and pick what you need.

steps.title: Wristbands decide your counters

state.caption: Your wristband opens some counters, not all

steps.narration: Every diner wears a **wristband**. Yours opens the salad bar and the grill stall, but not the custom-order desk. A brand-new dish that no wristband covers sits in the kitchen where nobody can order it. It exists, but to every diner it's invisible.

callout.text: A dish nobody's wristband covers might as well not exist; that's the #1 'my catalog is missing' cause.

whatChanged: ~ new dish: no band covers it

steps.title: Order ticket, then the manager signs

state.caption: No cooking until the ticket is signed

steps.narration: You write what you want on an **order ticket** and hand it in. Before anyone spends money on it, your manager reads the ticket and signs it off. Only a signed ticket moves on to the people who actually buy the food.

steps.title: Expediter, supplier, and the real words
steps.narration: Pre-agreed dishes go straight to the supplier; everything else goes through an **expediter** first. Now the real terms: kitchen = **procurement BU**, wristband = **content zone**, ticket = **requisition**, sign-off = **approval**, expediter = **buyer**, supplier order = **purchase order (PO)**. Agreements let approved lines become POs with no buyer touch [S14] [S16].

callout.text: The analogy breaks at invoices: there's no food-court version of 2-, 3- or 4-way matching.

whatChanged: ~ every object gets its real name

steps.title: Before anything: the right BU
steps.narration: The pipeline has six stages, but a requester can't even enter without data access to an active **business unit (BU)** that has the **Requisitioning** business function. Without it, the app shows error `POR-2010674` [S5]. Your **Preferences** then set the default requisitioning BU, deliver-to location and charge account [S6].

steps.title: Shop: one search over all content
steps.narration: In **Purchase Requisitions (New)** you search or browse [S10]. One search covers local catalogs, punchout catalogs hosted by suppliers [S9] and **smart forms** for non-catalog requests [S8]. But content only shows up if a **content zone** covers you [S7]. Zones are the security layer between catalogs and requesters [S4].

callout.text: Creating a catalog does nothing for requesters until it's in a content zone [S7].

whatChanged: ~ local, punchout, smart form feed Shop

steps.title: Cart and submit
steps.narration: Add items to the cart, open it, and edit the details: delivery location, project, attachments. Then **Submit**; the requisition appears under My recent requisitions [S10]. From 25B the cart's **View Approvers** shows who will approve and the name of the rule that added each approver [S2].

steps.title: Approve: four stages in a row
steps.narration: Approval rules come from **Manage Requisition Approvals** [S11], which runs on the **Approval Management Extension (AMX)** rules engine [S12]. Four seeded stages run in order: **Header Preapproval**, **Header**, **Header Postapproval**, then **Postapproval FYI** [S11].

steps.title: Buyer: a precedence chain
steps.narration: Each line needs a **buyer**. If the requester suggested one, that wins. Otherwise the **buyer assignment rules** decide, then the item's default buyer, then the procurement BU's default buyer [S13]. The first source that gives an answer is used. Here the requester left it blank, so the rules decide.

steps.title: The switch: touchless PO

state.caption: Express track: straight to a PO

steps.narration: If the line comes from an agreement whose **Controls** tab has **Automatically generate orders**, the approved line becomes a PO by itself; **Automatically submit for approval** also submits it [S14]. The line also needs a valid buyer, a supplier and site, and **Negotiated** checked if it's from a contract agreement [S15].

callout.text: Pick only 'Automatically generate orders' (not auto-submit) for high-value items, so a buyer reviews the PO [S14].

steps.title: The siding: Process Requisitions

state.caption: Siding: the line waits for a buyer

steps.narration: Miss any condition, here **Negotiated**, and the line isn't converted [S15]. It waits in **Process Requisitions**. The buyer adds it to the **document builder**, picks document type, document style and line grouping, and creates the order [S16].

callout.text: 'Approved but no PO' is almost always one of these checklist items, not a stuck approval [S15].

steps.title: Edge case: invoice on hold
steps.narration: With **3-way match**, an invoice must agree with the PO and a receipt [S17]. Invoice 10, received 8: a **QTY REC** hold. For direct-delivery expense lines, the Redwood app flags it and the requester clicks **Confirm Receipt**, which creates the receipt [S18]. Flags appear only after the **Update Requisition Line Action Required Code** job runs [S18].

steps.title: Requisitioning BU vs Procurement BU
steps.narration: A **requisitioning BU** raises demand and holds requisition defaults, set in **Configure Requisitioning Business Function** [S3]. One or more **procurement BUs** serve it and turn demand into orders. If no procurement BU can be found from the line, the **Default Procurement BU** processes it [S3].

code.title: Setup task
code.src:
Setup and Maintenance
  > Configure Requisitioning Business Function
    Default Procurement BU
    Default Deliver-to Organization
    Cancel Unfulfilled Demand

whatChanged: + two req BUs, two proc BUs

steps.title: Content zones: usage and security

state.caption: A zone hangs off one procurement BU

steps.narration: A content zone belongs to one procurement BU and has one usage [S4]. **Requisitioning** zones are secured by requisitioning BU, by worker, or by deliver-to location; **Available to all procurement users** exists only for procurement usage [S4]. The requester's BU must be a client of the zone's procurement BU [S4]. Unzoned content is invisible [S7].

code.title: Setup task
code.src:
Setup and Maintenance
  > Manage Content Zones
    Usage: Requisitioning
    Secured by: Requisitioning BU | Worker | Deliver-to location

steps.title: Approval rules vs task settings
steps.narration: Rules are authored in **Manage Requisition Approvals**, each with a list builder: Supervisory, Position, Job Level, Single User, User-Defined Routing or Approval Groups [S11]. They run on **AMX**. Task behavior lives in **BPM Worklist** Task Configuration: by default aggregation is **Once per task** and the task completes on **Reject** [S12].

callout.text: Looking for rules in BPM Worklist is a classic dead end; BPM only configures the task [S12].

code.title: Setup task
code.src:
Rules:  Setup and Maintenance > Manage Requisition Approvals
Task:   BPM Worklist > Task Configuration
        (aggregation, completion, who can add participants)

steps.title: Serial vs parallel routing

state.caption: Header stage, three approvers in parallel

steps.narration: Participants route in **serial**, one after another up a hierarchy, or in **parallel** [S11]. Parallel has two voting styles. **Consensus**: every approver must approve. **First Responder Wins**: the first response decides the stage [S11]. Here one approval completes the Header stage.

code.title: Setup task
code.src:
Manage Requisition Approvals
  > Header stage > participant
    Routing: Serial | Parallel
    Voting:  Consensus | First Responder Wins

steps.title: Touchless PO checklist

state.caption: All green: the line goes express

steps.narration: The agreement's **Business Unit Access** must include the requisitioning BU and supplier site; its **Controls** need Automatically generate orders [S14]. The line needs a valid buyer, supplier and site, an item purchasable in the procurement BU's inventory org, and **Negotiated** for contract-agreement lines [S15]. With consolidation on, the PO waits for **Generate Orders** [S15].

code.title: Setup task
code.src:
Purchase Agreement
  > Business Unit Access: requisitioning BU + supplier site
  > Controls: Automatically generate orders
             Automatically submit for approval (optional)

steps.title: Match levels and the Redwood switch
steps.narration: **2-way** matches PO and invoice; **3-way** adds the receipt; **4-way** adds inspection-accepted quantity, each within tolerance [S17]. Separately, the Redwood app is switched on by opt-in: **Redwood as default** for everyone, or phased with `POR_MANAGE_REQ_WITH_PWA_PRIV` [S1] [S2]. First use needs **Elastic Search** set up [S1].

callout.text: Match approval level is independent of the invoice match option (PO vs receipt) [S17].

whatChanged: ~ 26A added barcode search and Check Funds [S19]

quiz.q: A requester gets `POR-2010674` when opening Purchase Requisitions (New). What fixes it?
options: Assign them the Procurement Agent job role
Grant access to an active requisitioning BU
Add them to a requisition approval group
Rebuild the requisition Elastic Search index
quiz.why: The error means the user has no access to a BU with the Requisitioning business function; fix it in Manage Business Unit Data Access for Users [S5].

quiz.q: A new local catalog is invisible to every requester. What is the most likely cause?
options: It isn't in a content zone covering them
It has no default buyer set on it
The approval rule for it isn't deployed yet
quiz.why: Content stays invisible until a catalog administrator associates it with a content zone that covers the requester [S7] [S4].

quiz.q: Where do you author requisition approval rules?
quiz.why: Rules live in Manage Requisition Approvals on the AMX engine [S11]; BPM Worklist only holds task settings such as aggregation [S12].

quiz.q: In a parallel stage set to First Responder Wins, what happens?
options: The first response decides the stage
Approvers act one by one in hierarchy order
quiz.why: Consensus needs all approvers; First Responder Wins lets the first response decide [S11].

quiz.q: Which source decides a requisition line's buyer first?
options: The procurement BU's default buyer setting
quiz.why: A requester-suggested buyer wins; only then do rules, the item default and the procurement BU default apply [S13].

quiz.q: An approved line sourced from a contract agreement has no PO, though the agreement has Automatically generate orders. Likely cause?
options: Negotiated isn't checked on the line
The catalog isn't in a content zone
The match level is set to 2-way
quiz.why: Lines sourced to a contract agreement need Negotiated checked, or automation skips them [S15].

quiz.q: What does 3-way match require that 2-way match doesn't?
quiz.why: 3-way adds the receipt to PO and invoice; 4-way adds inspection [S17].
